en: It glided like a snake,
And when locked in close struggle,
It never yielded in the least;
It bore every mark of a thoroughbred.
When seen among the people,
Sarala with its stake-straight neck
Was made to arch proudly by Almambet;
Sarala with its slender tail
Was made to quiver by Almambet;
Sarala with its cow-like croup
Was made to whirl by Almambet.
Kongurbay of the infidels
Was then standing there watching.
Almambet, son of Khan Azozyl,
Was about to ask Manas for the joust
And meet his death there.
"Panther Manas, my soul's friend,
Please consent to what I ask.
The Kalmyk has come out to joust;
Give this joust to me.
He too was a khan's son,
And I too was a khan's son.
Let us joust with spears
And satisfy our hearts' longing.
Please consent to what I ask;
The joust against Kongurbay,
My friend Manas, give it to me.
Please agree to these words of mine.
He was a fellow who wore
The Chinese robe, broad and red-flowered,
Alongside me;
From childhood we stood opposed
And constantly provoked each other.
Since we were sons of elder and younger brothers,
He was a fellow always beside me.
Kongurbay, son of Alooke—
Our forefather was Chylaba;
Over Chylaba's tea mine
He was a fellow who quarreled with me.
I have a grievance against that pig:
My land of Beijing that I had won,
Kongurbay took away,
Along with my gold-bearing mine.
He scattered, divided, and destroyed
The people who looked to me.
If you truly are my friend,
Hear my words, Manas.
From that day until this one
I have been unable to take my revenge.
I have been unable to see Beijing,
Chinmachin, or Kakan.
My true friend Manas, grant this to me;
When else shall I see your support?"
When Almambet had spoken so,
Great-hearted Manas replied:
"Ah, Alake, my gray wolf,
Would the black Chinese and Manchu people
Not consume us with their slander?
Would they not say, 'When Khan Azozyl's only son
Fled and came to the Buruts,
They mercilessly handed him over
To be put to death'?
Would the Chinese not mock us,
Would God not strike down my land?
Would the fortune of this gray wolf Almambet
Not be broken by this deed?
The Chinese would turn it into a legend;
Would God not strike us for it?
Would they not gnaw at our very core,
Saying, 'That wandering Chinese man
They handed over to death'?
Would they not say, 'The patterned spear in his hand
At last failed him'?
Would they not say that Manas
And all the assembled Buruts
Spared him from Kongurbay?
Would they not say that to Kokotoy's feast
Almambet came as a fugitive,
Fleeing and wandering?
Would they not say that all the Buruts gathered
And Almambet's punishment
Was carried out by them?"
"Oh Almambet, my soul's friend,
If you go out to joust,
This act of yours will bring shame.
If you truly are my friend,
Stand aside and watch impartially.
Lay down your agitation
And be our support.
Consent to what I say.
Sarala beneath you
Is a beast fit to ride into combat;
Give us the use of its strength.
If you give Sarala's strength,
We shall ride your swift horse.
Against that dog who boasts of strength
I shall clash and test myself.
He has mounted Algara
And has grown boastful of his valor.
Against that boastful dog
I shall meet chest to chest.
Against that dog who boasts of strength
Let me see how our clash will end!"
The hero Manas, the panther,
Before all the people, from Almambet
Asked for Sarala.
Almambet restrained his anger
And surrendered Sarala.
To the hero Manas, the gray wolf,
Unable to say, "I will not give it,"
And unwilling to reject the hero's wish,
He consented to what Manas said
And gave Sarala, bright as moonlight,
To his great-hearted lord.
Upon Sarala
Was Alake's white saddle;
Three girths and three cruppers—
He loosened all six,
And removed the white saddle.
Taking off its tack and leaving it bareback,
He took a shortcut down a narrow path,
Leading Almambet's Sarala
Along entirely bareback.
The gray sash that fell from the sky
Was wrapped around his slender waist;
The panther touched by Kydyr
Prayed to the Almighty.
In fury he made himself ready,
And buckled on Zulpukor,
The six blades that fell from heaven.
The lionlike gray-wolf panther
Moved with ringing confidence,
Holding the warrior Kongur he would fight
As worth no more than the hem of his robe.
He gave no thought to where it might end,
And never thought, "I shall die."
When the great host of dark-clad Muslims
Looked on, their hearts were stirred.
The panther's guardian spirit
Appeared like a snow-covered mountain;
Nine protectors appeared
On his right side,
And nine supporters appeared,
Bearing the likeness of takers of souls.
The blood-drinking lion was enraged,
Truly seized by his thirst for blood.
When one looked upon his front,
His eyes blazed like a lion's;
He charged like a tiger,
And none he struck could remain alive.
He frowned darkly in wrath—
Such was the panther's state.
From the giants Koshoy and Toshtuk,
From Azhybai and Khan Bakai,
With palms raised, saying "Amen,"
He stood asking their blessing.
The two khans, Bakai and Koshoy,
Hung their belts around their necks;
Raising their palms and saying "Amen,"
They prayed to the Almighty:
"O Almighty, amen!
His fortune has always been complete.
God, cast the infidel beneath him;
God, raise Manas above him.
He is the lion upheld by the patron spirit;
Creator, hear my words
And do not let my back be broken.
God, grant victory
To my panther Manas, my lion.
Do not raise the Chinese above us,
Do not cast the Kyrgyz beneath them.
The morning star stands in the sky;
God, do not scatter those behind him.
If You created the black Kalmyks and Manchus
As living souls, O God,
Do not let their eyes ever look straight upon him.
If by mischance he falls from his horse,
The lion prince, the panther,
If by accident he should fall,
They stand ready to write the line,
'He delivered his Manas into our hands.'
With Khan Kongurbay at their head,
Against the Muslim people
They stand ready to make a spectacle.
Do not let the Chinese day dawn;
If You created my people as living souls,
Do not let them be slaughtered
And driven back toward their homeland.
The black Kalmyks and Manchus
Have a migrating host they once shattered,
And have long borne a grudge against us.
If Manas were no longer before their eyes,
The arrogant heroes' heads
They yearn to take with their swords;
The Chinese go about nursing vengeance,
Longing to bring slaughter upon us.
This infidel has a fearsome look
And has long been possessed by rage.
The Chinese eagerly seek
To bind and capture the faithful,
And to make all the Muslims
Into slave laborers.
The ravenous black Chinese—
If people like us fall into their hands,
Their custom is to slaughter every one.
At Kokotoy's memorial feast
We have happened to gather together.
Make this an age that finds its meaning;
If You created us as living souls, O God,
Keep Manas safe for us.
Oh Khan Manas, my dear colt!"
So then the Muslims prayed;
The elders Koshoy and Bakai,
Those saints, gave their blessing.
Raising their hands and sobbing,
The handful of Muslims
Loudly cried out their blessing.
The Muslims stood in an uproar:
Is not Manas the backbone
That braces the Kyrgyz waist?
Unshaken and courageous,
Is not Manas their lion?
Is it not Manas who brought slaughter
Across the whole wide world?
Is it not Manas who freed
All of the Muslims
From the black Chinese and Manchus
And gathered them beneath his hand?
Looming like Opol-Too,
Your saintly gray wolf Manas
Grew wrathful and made himself ready;
The blood-drinker Manas mounted his horse.
Twenty rode on his right,
Worthy comrades, matchless men;
Twenty rode on his left,
Bodyguard companions of the blood-drinker,
Matchless men who brought devastation.
Kalkaman's Black Horse
The blood-drinker had mounted,
While cow-rumped Sarala
Was led beside him bareback.
All of those master riders
As though ready to come to his aid,
They held out their spears
And stood as his support.
The finest of the forty companions,
The most skillful of spearmen,
The very strongest heroes,
The blaze-headed thoroughbreds among horses—
Almambet and Chubak among them,
With Khan Agybay and Bakai there—
They stood in support then;
All the falcons were there.
If Manas dismounted,
The leopards Almambet and Chubak
Would reach him before he could open his eyes.
